questions.title: What distinguishes 'intrinsic' evidence from 'propensity' evidence under Rule 404(b) in the context of ongoing firearm possession?
questions.question_body: In *United States v. Cutbank*, the court ruled that testimony showing the defendant possessed the same sawed-off rifle on previous occasions was 'intrinsic evidence' rather than impermissible character/propensity evidence under Rule 404(b). I am struggling to understand the precise boundary here. Usually, evidence of past bad acts is excluded to show disposition. Why does proof of prior possession of the *exact same* weapon automatically fall into the 'intrinsic' exception, and how does this differ from a scenario where a defendant is charged with possession but witnesses say they saw him with a *different* gun years ago? Does 'continuous possession' negate the need for a 404(b) analysis entirely?

questions.title: Does a witness's personal tragedy (e.g., sibling killed by a gun) constitute inadmissible character evidence or permissible impeachment context?
questions.question_body: During cross-examination about inconsistent statements regarding the gun, the witness (D.F.) explained her memory gaps by stating she 'did not like guns' because her sister was killed by one. The defense moved to strike this, arguing prejudice under Rule 403, but the court denied it. I don't see how D.F.'s family history makes her testimony about *Cutbank's* actions more credible or relevant to the elements of the crime. Isn't this just introducing emotional baggage to sway the jury against the defendant? How does this pass Rule 403 balancing when it seems designed solely to elicit sympathy or bias?

questions.title: Can extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements be introduced if the document itself lacks proper authentication?
questions.question_body: The defense tried to cross-examine witness C.F. using a police report containing her prior statements, but the court blocked them from reading parts of it because C.F. didn't author the report (it was written by an officer). The appellate court upheld this, citing *United States v. Cumbie*. My confusion lies in the procedure: If C.F. admits she made those statements orally, why is an unauthenticated police report required for extrinsic evidence? Is there a distinction between impeaching via oral questioning versus introducing a document, and does this rule effectively prevent defendants from using official reports to challenge witness credibility even when the witness doesn't deny making them?

questions.title: How does USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) interact with ACCA enhancements when both rely on similar underlying conduct?
questions.question_body: The defendant was convicted under ACCA (Armed Career Criminal Act) due to three prior violent felonies, yet he also received a four-level enhancement under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for possessing a firearm 'in connection with another felony offense.' The opinion notes that ACCA triggers statutory minimums while guidelines calculate offense levels, but I'm confused about double counting or redundancy. Specifically, if the 'other felony' used for the guideline enhancement is part of the current charge (domestic assault/kidnapping), isn't that inherent in every felon-in-possession case involving violence? What specific element separates an ACCA conviction from satisfying § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), and can these run concurrently without violating principles against duplicative punishment?

questions.title: Is an explicit recitation of § 3553(a) factors required for every sentence within-the-guidelines range?
questions.question_body: Cutbank argued that his sentence conflicted with § 3553(a)'s requirement that punishment be 'sufficient but not greater than necessary,' claiming the district court failed to adequately weigh these factors despite imposing a within-range sentence. The Eighth Circuit affirmed based on *Maluoth*, stating courts need not provide a 'mechanical recitation.' Given that Cutbank had numerous violent priors and committed severe acts during this incident, at what point does a judge's silence on specific § 3553(a) factors become reversible error? Is there any scenario where a within-range sentence is presumed unreasonable solely because the judge didn't verbally list every factor they considered?

questions.title: When is failure to request a limiting instruction regarding hearsay considered waived or harmless error?
questions.question_body: The defense requested an instruction telling jurors they couldn't use D.F.'s out-of-court statements as substantive proof until she testified in person. The district court declined, noting D.F. eventually testified anyway and Confrontation Clause rights were satisfied upon her appearance. I'm confused about the timing: If hearsay was admitted earlier without limitation, isn't that prejudicial regardless of later testimony? Under what circumstances can an appellate court deem it 'harmless error' to admit hearsay without a contemporaneous limiting instruction if no objection was raised at that exact moment?
